{{Short description|Two congruent circles within an arbelos}}
[[File:Archimedes' Circles.svg|thumb|400px|right|The twin circles (red) of an arbelos (grey)]]

In [[geometry]], the '''twin circles''' are two special circles associated with an [[arbelos]].
An arbelos is determined by three collinear points {{mvar|A}}, {{mvar|B}}, and {{mvar|C}}, and is the curvilinear triangular region between the three [[semicircle]]s that have {{mvar|AB}}, {{mvar|BC}}, and {{mvar|AC}} as their diameters. If the arbelos is partitioned into two smaller regions by a line segment through the middle point of {{mvar|A}}, {{mvar|B}}, and {{mvar|C}}, perpendicular to line {{mvar|ABC}}, then each of the two twin circles lies within one of these two regions, tangent to its two semicircular sides and to the splitting segment.

These circles first appeared in the ''[[Book of Lemmas]]'', which showed (Proposition V) that the two circles are [[congruence (geometry)|congruent]].<ref name=archBLprop5/>
[[Thābit ibn Qurra]], who translated this book into Arabic,  attributed it to [[Ancient Greece|Greek]] mathematician [[Archimedes]]. Based on this claim the twin circles, and several other circles in the Arbelos congruent to them, have also been called '''Archimedes's circles'''. However, this attribution has been questioned by later scholarship.<ref>{{cite journal| last=Boas | first=Harold P.| author-link1=Harold P. Boas | title=Reflections on the Arbelos | journal=[[The American Mathematical Monthly]] | year=2006| volume=113| issue=3| url=http://www.maa.org/programs/maa-awards/writing-awards/reflections-on-the-arbelos| pages=241| doi=10.1080/00029890.2006.11920301| s2cid=14528513|quote=The source for the claim that Archimedes studied and named the arbelos is the ''Book of Lemmas'', also known as the ''Liber assumptorum'' from the title of the seventeenth century Latin translation of the ninth-century Arabic translation of the lost Greek original. Although this collection of fifteen propositions is included in standard editions of the works of Archimedes, the editors acknowledge that the author of the ''Book of Lemmas'' was not Archimedes but rather some anonymous later compiler, who indeed refers to Archimedes in the third person| url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Construction==
[[File:Круги-близнецы.gif|thumb|right|Animation of twin circles for various positions of point B on AC segment]]

Specifically, let <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, and <math>C</math> be the three corners of the arbelos, with <math>B</math> between <math>A</math> and <math>C</math>.  Let <math>D</math> be the point where the larger semicircle intercepts the line [[perpendicular]] to the <math>AC</math> through the point <math>B</math>.  The segment <math>BD</math> divides the arbelos in two parts.  The twin circles are the two circles inscribed in these parts, each [[tangent]] to one of the two smaller semicircles, to the segment <math>BD</math>, and to the largest semicircle.<ref name=wolframArbelos/>

Each of the two circles is uniquely determined by its three tangencies.  Constructing it is a special case of the [[Problem of Apollonius]].

Alternative approaches to constructing two circles congruent to the twin circles have also been found.<ref name=lamoenCat/><ref name=lamoenDao/> These circles have also been called Archimedean circles. They include the [[Bankoff circle]], [[Schoch circles]], and [[Woo circles]].

==Properties==
Let ''a'' and ''b'' be the diameters of two inner semicircles, so that the outer semicircle has diameter ''a''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''b''.  The diameter of each twin circle is then<ref name=wolframArbelos/>

:<math>d=\frac{ab}{a+b}.</math>

Alternatively, if the outer semicircle has unit diameter, and the inner circles have diameters <math>s</math> and <math>1-s</math>, the diameter of each twin circle is<ref name=wolframArbelos/>
:<math>d=s(1-s). \, </math>

The smallest circle that encloses both twin circles has the same area as the arbelos.<ref name=wolframArbelos/>
